nameStory: The boxwood mite gets its name from its favorite host plant - the boxwood shrub that's beloved by gardeners for hedges and topiaries. This tiny arachnid has developed such a close relationship with boxwood that it's rarely found anywhere else, making it the boxwood's unwelcome but devoted companion.
description: Boxwood mites are incredibly tiny spider mites that you'll rarely see with the naked eye - they're smaller than the period at the end of this sentence! These microscopic arachnids are pale yellow to light green in color and have the typical spider mite body shape: oval and somewhat flattened. At full size, they measure less than 0.5mm long, making them among the smallest arachnids you might encounter in New England gardens.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Impossibly tiny - smaller than a pinhead and barely visible without magnification. Hold a magnifying glass close to suspected leaves to spot these microscopic movers.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Oval and slightly flattened like a tiny seed, with a soft, translucent appearance that makes them look almost jewel-like under magnification.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Pale yellow to light green coloration that can appear almost colorless. Look for two dark spots on the back which are actually their body contents showing through.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates extremely fine webbing that feels almost sticky when you brush against infested boxwood leaves. The webbing catches light like gossamer threads.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in slow, deliberate steps across leaf surfaces. When disturbed, they tend to freeze in place rather than scurrying away quickly.

habitat: Found exclusively on boxwood shrubs in New England gardens, parks, and landscaped areas. They prefer the undersides of boxwood leaves where humidity is higher and they're protected from direct sunlight. You'll most commonly encounter them in formal gardens, foundation plantings, and anywhere boxwood hedging is used for landscaping.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to feed and reproduce on new boxwood growth. Look for the first signs of fine webbing on branch tips.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with multiple generations developing rapidly in hot weather. Webbing becomes most noticeable, and leaf damage appears as stippling or bronzing.
seasonality.fall: Activity slows as temperatures drop, but mites continue feeding until first frost. Late-season populations prepare for winter by moving to protected areas.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in bark crevices and under loose bark scales on boxwood stems, becoming dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: A single female boxwood mite can lay up to 100 eggs in her lifetime, and in ideal summer conditions, she can go from egg to reproducing adult in just one week - meaning populations can explode faster than almost any other arachnid!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other spider mites, but boxwood mites are found almost exclusively on boxwood plants. If you're seeing tiny mites on roses, tomatoes, or other plants, you're likely looking at two-spotted spider mites instead. Memory trick: 'Boxwood mites stick to boxwood - they're plant-faithful!'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'mites,' these are true arachnids in the spider mite family, not the parasitic mites that bite humans or pets. They're plant feeders that pose no direct threat to people, though they can seriously damage valuable boxwood landscaping if left unchecked.
compareHints: Since boxwood mites are the only Eurytetranychus species commonly found in New England, compare them with two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) which are more common but larger and found on many different plants. Boxwood mites are smaller, paler, and strictly boxwood-specific, while two-spotted mites are darker with visible spots and attack a wide variety of garden plants.
